title: Queue Built From Two Stacks
statement:
Build a first-in, first-out queue using only stacks. A stack here is an array you may only push to the end, pop from the end, read at the end, and ask for its length. No shifting, no indexing from the front.

  • MyQueue() creates an empty queue.
  • push(x) adds x to the back.
  • pop() removes and returns the value at the front.
  • peek() returns the value at the front without removing it.
  • empty() returns whether the queue holds no values.

pop and peek are only called on a non-empty queue. Aim for amortized O(1) per operation.

Tests list the operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the queue. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: 4 went in first, so it is both at the front and the first one out. 9 is still waiting.
3 arrives after 2 has already been moved over for the first pop. It must still come out after 2.

constraints: pop and peek are never called on an empty queue
hints: Pouring a stack into another stack reverses it. What does the oldest value become after the pour?
Use one stack for incoming values and one for outgoing values. Where should pop look first?
Only pour from the inbox into the outbox when the outbox is empty. Each value then moves at most once, so the total work stays linear.

explain.intuition:
A stack hands values back newest first. Pour all of its values into a second stack and the order flips: the oldest value ends up on top. That is the queue order you want.

The trick is to pour lazily. Keep an inbox for pushes and an outbox for pops. pop and peek read the outbox; only when it is empty do you pour the whole inbox across. Values already in the outbox are older than anything in the inbox, so they must leave first, which is why you never pour into a non-empty outbox. Each value is pushed and popped at most twice in total, so any sequence of operations costs O(1) per call on average. Message queues built from two buffers, such as a double-buffered render list, follow the same plan.
steps: peek(): if outbox is empty, pop every value from inbox and push it onto outbox. Return the top of outbox.
pop(): call peek() to make sure the outbox is filled, then pop and return its top.
empty(): return whether both stacks are empty.
pitfalls: Pouring the inbox into the outbox while the outbox still has values. Newer values then jump ahead of older ones, as the second example checks.
Pouring back from the outbox to the inbox after every pop. Correct, but it costs O(n) per operation.
empty() checking only one of the two stacks.

solutions.title: Keep one stack in queue order
solutions.idea: On each push, move everything to a helper stack, push the new value at the bottom, and move everything back. The front stays on top.
solutions.time: O(n) per push, O(1) for the rest

solutions.title: Inbox and outbox, pour lazily
solutions.idea: Push to the inbox. Pop and peek from the outbox, refilling it from the inbox only when it runs empty.

followups: Amortized O(1) still allows one slow call. Can you bound the worst case of a single pop?
Now build a stack using only queues. Which operation becomes the expensive one?
